For several years, the task of forecast predicting customer churn has drawn significant interest from industry leaders and academia due to its importance in retaining customers and increasing revenue. Most effective models developed to address this task rely on sequence-based input methods such as recurrent neural networks (RNNs), which analyze sequence-length time-windowed features to forecast future behavior. Nevertheless, the input sequences used for training these models influence both their capabilities and outcomes because the complexity of the issues they pose varies significantly. Notably, the relative merits of input sequences both length and type remain poorly comprehended despite their varied influence on task difficulty and model performance. Consequently, the aim of this study is to investigate how the utilization of different input sequences impacts the performance and insights gained from supervised learning models. Notably, the results indicate that the time-series history used for training these models impacts both the quality and consistency of the models. Furthermore, the investigation showcases a novel method for selecting the most suitable input sequence automatically and highlights its advantages. The methods and findings discussed here were validated using a dataset of customer churn, which was derived from real-life digital transactions.

We examine the impact of an irrelevant operator $L_{-4}\bar{L}_{-4}\eta$ on the integrability of the effective theory in the Ising Field Theory with a small $\eta$ parameter, where $\eta$ represents a minor deviation from the magnetic field threshold. Utilizing the reormalization group framework and integrating the RG flow up to the ultraviolet limit, we analyze the dynamic behavior of the magnetic susceptibility and specific heat. Our analysis reveals that the integration of the RG flow reveals spin precession and spin wave behaviors following the RG flow, which are distinct from the spin waves observed in the magnetic field threshold limit. We observe that the spin precession and wave behaviors emerge on separate scales related to powers of $\eta$. Our analytical results are validated by the numerical simulations of the 1D Ising model.

In the context of lattice calculations, we explore factorization formulas that link renormalized gluon TMDPDFs across various schemes, including those with power-counting hints and F-space relationships. By combining the systematic use of vertex resummation and the decoupling approach, we rigorously establish the connection between the APDF and \bar{q}PDF frameworks, as well as between the \bar{q}PDF and gluon PDF frameworks, under the momentum-space dispersion relation. We find that the F-space relationship holds strictly in the large-$N_c$ limit, while discrepancies arise for $N_c=3$ due to the differences between the Mellin transform and the large-$N_c$ limit in the operator product expansion. Our findings suggest that these discrepancies will not significantly affect the lattice calculations utilizing the large-$N_c$ approximation.

The underlying physics of electron-positron pair production in high-energy collisions between heavy ions has been extensively examined using theoretical models, except for the impact of strong electromagnetic fields on this process. In the context of ultra-relativistic collisions, our study uses the classical Dirac equation to simulate the creation of electron-positron pairs from collisions between small nuclei and protons, while accounting for the influence of collective electromagnetic fields through the Unsold approximation. Our research employs the classical electromagnetic model and the Landau distribution to describe the initial conditions, electromagnetic fields, and electron/proton motion, respectively. Our results reveal the significant impact of collective electromagnetic fields on the spatial distribution, directed flow, and yield of electron-positron pairs at midrapidity. Notably, the significance of this impact varies depending on the rapidity and transverse momentum of the parent particles.

The rapidly growing popularity of urban cycling necessitates the improvement of safety measures to accommodate the increasing number of users. While there is an abundance of information available for vehicle operators, there is a significant knowledge gap when it comes to cyclists. One effective way to address this issue is by leveraging monitoring cyclist data, which can offer valuable insights to inform the development of enhanced safety systems for urban cyclists. In this study, we introduce a novel cycling detection algorithm that utilizes data from intelligent traffic signals to identify safe cycling behaviors. The approach entails a two-step process of detecting and classifying cyclists based on anatomical segment data. Evaluations of the methodology reveal an overall detection efficiency of 85% and an overall classification efficiency of 81%, providing a foundation for future research on refining the classification system. Once refined, this system can be used to track individual cyclists equipped with wearable technology, enabling real-time safety feedback and informing the development of predictive models to prevent recurring incidents.

This research introduces a robust path planning framework for robotic systems, taking into account uncertainties in their environmental models. By formulation, the path planning problem is redefined as an uncertainty quantified optimization issue, aiming to find a path that holds up against model inaccuracies while minimizing its impact. A zero-expectation stochastic gradient method is proposed to tackle this challenge, demonstrating rapid and practical convergence. Furthermore, the framework can adapt to changing environmental conditions and scale up efficiently for complex robotic applications. Through numerical analysis on a multi-robot navigation example, the effectiveness and efficiency of the proposed approach are substantiated.

We establish that the covering number of a ring without unity is equal to the covering number of its unital form when augmented with an identity element. Consequently, several key characteristics and coverings of rings without unity can be reduced to their unital counterparts. Specifically, we demonstrate that the (H)BK-cocovering number, (H)BK-cocovering number, Arkha-Tzamzumin number, and Hilbert-basis number of a ring without unity are all equivalently defined for its unital form. In related work, we show that every ring without unity can be transformed into its unital form by identifying an additional element, such that the coverings of the two rings are equivalent. Furthermore, we expand upon a theorem by Bouslimani, establishing that certain rings without unity satisfy the Bouslimani property if, essentially, every unital ring corresponding to it contains an ideal that, when added to the ring, makes it satisfy a specific congruence condition. Additionally, we introduce the notion of topological rings without unity and derive equivalents to several topological ring characteristics for their unital forms.

Neural networks employing straight-forward mapping strategies are interesting due to their relatively minimal capacity for complexity. Yet, intriguingly, adding such strategies to well-performing baseline models actually increases their susceptibility to adversarial attacks. In this study, a new adversarial example generation approach is proposed, focusing on exploiting specific vulnerabilities in neural networks incorporating straight-forward mapping strategies. By assessing the differences in error between straight-forward mapping models and a baseline discriminator in a multi-task setup, the proposed method reduces high-error regions that are indicative of adversarial vulnerabilities. The proposed strategy outperforms existing methods by generating more transferable adversarial examples, demonstrating its effectiveness on multiple benchmark datasets, including MNIST and CIFAR-10.

This research investigates a class of convolution kernels with bounded variation that lead a wide range of nonlocal solutions of conservation laws to statistically consistent solutions. By employing a quantitative estimate of solution stability, this study provides the most general stability and convergence result for statistically consistent solutions up to this point. A distinctive aspect of this work is that it requires minimal assumptions about the initial data and solution properties. The investigation also includes an assessment of convolution kernel properties that are essential for solution convergence and a discussion on the applicability of these properties to various kernels, including those with singularities. A notable example considered in this work is the kernel associated with the Fourier multiplier operator, for which proving convergence remains an open question.

We investigate the dynamics of hyperbolic surfaces within the unit tangent bundle of a finite area surface. A comprehensive analysis is provided for the case of a closed geodesic. Under the assumption that the geodesic is not weakly pseudo-Anosov, we demonstrate that the directions in which it rotates form a dense set within the unit circle. By establishing relationships with questions regarding the generic nature of growth rates in topological entropy, we resolve two queries posed by Simon and Wolf, confirming that the surface's entropy is indeed finite when the geodesic is not weakly pseudo-Anosov. A step towards addressing the remaining scenario where the geodesic is weakly pseudo-Anosov is taken, along with an introduction to related problems.

Our understanding of brain connectivity can be enhanced by measuring the underlying correlations between neural signals, leading to more precise mapping of the brain's structural and functional organization. Recent research reveals that Total Correlation, a measure of underlying correlations, can serve as an indicator of brain alterations or conditions. To utilize Total Correlation in a brain imaging framework, we developed a Sparsity-based Estimation Technique (SSET) that makes it possible to recover underlying correlation maps from a limited set of raw signal data. By building upon the principles of Modern Cross-Correlation, SSET involves three key steps: forming a correlation matrix, defining a sparsity-enforcing constraint, and solving an optimization problem to produce the Total Correlation map. Notably, our proposed framework can recover the Total Correlation map with minimal data and without fully sampling the underlying signal correlations, making it a valuable tool for various applications. To evaluate the effectiveness and adaptability of our approach, we conducted comprehensive simulations across diverse signal types and data conditions and found that our method surpasses alternative techniques in recovering the Total Correlation map, particularly those that utilize sparse underlying signals.

This paper introduces a concept of $L^2$ space comprised of Clifford algebra-valued functions, defining it through an integration process and demonstrating its equivalence to a function modulated by a Clifford algebra element, modulo a set of functions that are zero on a certain measure set. This establishment is based on a specific relationship involving the sign of elements in higher-dimensional spaces, $N$ being an odd number. As a result, in scenarios where $N$ is even, a factor involving the square root of $-1$ is absent from the modulation. This concept enables expansion into modulated versions of spinor fields and the integration methods they utilize.

We develop a framework for conditioning Gaussian processes based on discrete paths without deriving the global posterior distribution, enabling efficient sampling of approximated posteriors with significantly reduced computational and memory requirements compared to traditional surrogate models. Our approximation can be viewed as a heuristic variant of Monte Carlo stochastic collocation methods and leverages analytical and numerical techniques to enhance sampling efficiency. The utility of this method is demonstrated through several numerical trials in the fields of uncertainty quantification for predictive modeling and inverse analysis. Notably, the method proves particularly valuable in inverse analysis, where it facilitates iterative Monte Carlo methods to iteratively converge to the global posterior distribution, often experiencing a tenfold increase in efficiency over typical implementations.

Recent research utilizing Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) as aerial base stations aims to establish communication connectivity between the UAVs and ground sensors that are isolated from direct power sources. Predicting communication connectivity depends on calculating path loss between the UAVs and ground sensors, which is typically done by evaluating the signal strength. Among various path loss models available, some are empirical and statistical, requiring data collection for specific scenarios, while others are computational models that estimate the signal loss based on given parameters. The Two-Ray model stands out as a simplified path loss model that considers terrestrial and aerial environments separately, but its existing implementations are tailored to specific applications. To bridge this gap, we have adapted the Two-Ray model for communication connectivity analysis between UAVs and ground sensors, introducing distinct aerial and ground-specific signal attenuation rates. Our approach is evaluated through a simulation-based comparison with the Standard Outdoor Indoor and Outdoor model, which is widely applied in wireless communication studies. The evaluation process involves adjusting the model parameters to achieve an accurate match with the Two-Ray model, as calculated using the least-squares method. The results show that the Two-Ray model is effective in predicting the received signal power when the UAVs are highly elevated, which corresponds to the aerial environment. However, when the UAVs are positioned at lower altitudes, the receive signal power is better predicted by the Two-Ray model that incorporates ground-specific attenuation rates.

The DUNE Liquid Argon Time Projection Chamber will be located at Sanford Lab in South Dakota and as part of this, a far detector named LArPD will track the decay of protons. With a similar design, LArPD will contribute to finding evidence for protons decaying into neutrinos and anti-neutrinos in conjunction with DUNE's main detector. Due to its distant location from proton sources, the DUNE detector is very efficient at identifying proton decay. With advanced signal enhancement techniques and high-resolution detection, the DUNE proton decay search will have exceptional sensitivity, enabling the discovery of new physics with high probability, particularly for excluded lifetimes under $10^{28}$ seconds. Moreover, LArPD and the DUNE detector will conduct simultaneous and accurate measurements of neutrino oscillations, allowing for precise validation of theoretical models of neutrino behavior. As part of this, LArPD will focus on the $anti{\nu}_{\mu}3\nu$ process and help calculate interaction cross-sections with greater accuracy, an improvement over existing data with a claimed precision of 10 percent. In terms of statistics, LArPD will collect around $5\times10^{41}$ interactions per year, which is comparable to CERN's proton-feeding neutrino experiment with 20 times more data. With two decades of continuous recording, the DUNE proton decay search will have sufficient data to confirm or deny most theoretical models of neutrino behavior and improve our understanding of the

The Shapley framework has revolutionized our comprehension of feature significance within machine learning models by assigning value to individual features. However, traditional Shapley values are computationally impractical for most machine learning models, prompting researchers to develop novel approaches that approximate features' contributions. Notably, the approach developed by Nethery and Saeed quantifies feature importance by optimizing group performance with and without each feature, yet assumes features interact non-additively, making feature contributions unpredictable in scenarios where interactions are multiplicatively interdependent. In response, our study introduces a new approximation technique that incorporates Shapley values, effectively extending the Nethery and Saeed method to cases where features interact multiplicatively. Our proposed technique is implemented using a specific type of neural network, but its underlying ideas are universally applicable, offering a new avenue for estimating feature contributions in complex machine learning models. Our research demonstrates that the approximately computed Shapley values outperform other existing feature importance methods in domains ranging from natural language processing to bioinformatics.

This chapter delves into the theoretical underpinnings of Virtual Organization (VO) modeling and the role of VO templates, which serve as standardized blueprints for defining and deploying collaborative setups. By adapting the Service-oriented View-Expansion (SOVE) semantics, the research breaks down VO formation into the creation of three core entities: a VO, a client, and a service provider, with each defined by their respective views. Utilizing the SOVE semantics, the paper explores the concept of VO template abstraction and instantiates it with the ET-Mediator VO, which is then analyzed from different ontological and semantic perspectives. The findings present a new approach for VO template generalization and specialization, which is eventually tested in a VO setting. The research contributes to the understanding of VO development by viewing entity creations as combinations of abstractions and instantiations that follow specific patterns. The entity life cycles are viewed as developmental stages that are influenced by the presence of VO templates. The VO concept is positioned within the broader context of Service-oriented communities, with a distinction drawn between static (organizationally-defined) and dynamic (agreement-based) Service-oriented communities. The research reveals that VO settings can evolve from static to dynamic forms, with implications for VO template design, VO configuration issues, and the role of VO templates in VO formation. The proposed VO entity life-cycle model is shown to capture VO entity characteristics at different stages of existence, with distinct characteristics distinguishing VO templates, VO instances, and the time periods when they exist

We've developed a variance reduction based experience replay framework, VRER, 
that employs a specially designed population dynamics model, PD-MAX, 
to optimize the reconstruction of the target Bellman operator in policy 
gradient methods. By leveraging the principles of Gaussian noise, VRER 
algorithmically explores a modified Markov decision process where the 
policy's value function is estimated with reduced variance. Utilizing 
our algorithmic framework, VRER is successfully applied to maximize the 
expected reward in complex reinforcement learning tasks, such as 
high-dimensional policies in variant policies of Atari games and 
multiple objective maximization in the Vizdoom dataset.

Utilizing superbosonization, an advanced version of the Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation with superbosonization being based on a graph-extended technique, it's shown that this transformation equals superbosonization. Furthermore, graph-based superbosonization is also compared with a bosonization method that utilizes a supergraph expansion in order to prove the equality of superbosonization and graph-based superbosonization. It's notable that the equalities of these transformations hold regardless of whether a symmetric or anti-symmetric Hubbard-Stratonovic transformation is employed. It's also shown that the graph-based superbosonization method is effective in creating a superbosonization graph expansion in which all terms are arranged in a supergraph expansion.

The Detail Context Block, a proposed module for spatiotemporal learning, effectively incorporates detail-level context from multiple viewpoints using a convolutional and shifting operation scheme.  To enhance the capture of moving objects, our Detail Context Block employs shifting operations with respect to predefined prototype positions.  By doing this, our Detail Context Block retrieves the details centered around the prototype for each detail level and views the video sequences from different angles, and then uses an adaptive fusion strategy to combine the contextual information.  Our Detail Context Block can be used as an efficient spatiotemporal feature extraction module for video classification, activity detection and other video-related tasks.  In our experiments, our Detail Context Block, when fine-tuned from pre-trained Video BERT from the large-scale Kinetics-400 dataset, achieves state-of-the-art results for video classification and activity detection on challenging UCF101, UCF-101-24, and JHMDB datasets.

Imperative programming languages have fundamental security flaws that can be addressed through the implementation of a type system for ensuring memory safety and error handling. Despite being in use for decades, the abstract concepts of type systems make it challenging to design them without a unified theoretical foundation. This paper outlines a general model suitable for all high-level imperative languages, which serves as a solution to this issue. Our type system is distinctive due to its incorporation of error handling and memory management, classifying errors in both divisions and memory management based on their type. This model views error handling and memory management as separate components with distinct type systems, later combining them with a dynamic flow control framework that includes function calls and recursion. Ultimately, our type system provides a formal definition for the set of valid program types in imperative languages, facilitating the development of tools for verifying program correctness and detecting type-related errors.

This work introduces an innovative decoding approach for pre-transformed polar codes, specifically designed for short lengths, which accommodates various error-correcting checksums. Building upon previous findings, the proposed method addresses limitations in non-symmetric PCM decoding, enabling better performance, particularly when using minimal-sized checksums. Notably, the proposed approach surpasses the existing state-of-the-art for CRC-aided PCM codes, while providing comparable or superior results for non-corrected variants. Furthermore, the proposed algorithm demonstrates its efficacy across diverse PCM sizes and checksum lengths. Notably, the proposed approach, which exhibits moderate computational complexity, enables better performance, especially for shorter codes, which are commonly applied in practice.

The use of median and clipped-mean coaddition in combination with a quadratic limb darkening model for unsaturated exoplanet host stars often results in an irregularly shaped Point Spread Function (PSF) due to the inherent nonlinearity. This nonlinearity in image combination leads to an irregularly shaped PSF in the frequency domain, resulting in an irregular PSF shape in the spatial domain after Fourier transformation. Consequently, using a circular aperture to restore the PSF shape leads to the introduction of artificial high-frequency features not present in real images, which in turn cause inaccurate monolithic nonlinear least squares fitting and hence incorrect parameter determinations including the stellar radius, planet radius, and distance. Following the removal of nonlinearity, we demonstrate through both theoretical and practical experiments that using simple linear coaddition fails to restore the original PSF shape, whereas application of nonlinearity correction followed by linear coaddition successfully restores the original PSF, allowing for the determination of accurate parameters including the stellar radius, planet radius, and distance.

A more precise understanding of how stress concentrates at the tip of a crack tip is developed by analyzing the mechanical response of an elastic-perfectly brittle material placed under tensile loading. By modeling this material as a brittle layer on top of an elastic substrate with similar material properties, we create a notch which generates stress concentrations. Our model, which consists of two materials with different stiffnesses, allows for a more accurate examination of the geometrical irregularities in the notch. Our numerical simulations demonstrate that the initial fracture usually starts at an advanced stage of stress concentration within the notch, as opposed to at its initial tip. We attribute this phenomenon to the presence of a sharpening instability at the notch tip and propose a theory that explains its relationship to the initial fracture point. Moreover, we observed that the first fracture typically occurs when the maximum stress is reached at an intermediate notch radius, as opposed to both the sharper and blunter forms of the notch.

We introduce the notion of "imaginary surfaces" as a means to describe the behavior of stochastic processes in the unit disk, where the chordal Schramm–Loewner evolution (ChSLE) serves as a primary example. We establish an equivalent characterization of ChSLE by defining it as the imaginary form of certain holomorphic processes, focusing on those with three or more starting points within the unit disk. This dual representation facilitates efficient derivation of key ChSLE outcomes. We also utilize this characterization to develop new insights into Loewner equations, revealing a connection between ChSLE and three-point PDE systems. Building on this link, we obtain an explicit solution to the Loewner equation when driven by ChSLE, shedding light on the integrability of the equation. Furthermore, it allows us to develop new integrability conditions and solve other similar three-point PDE systems.

This study establishes the existence and distinctiveness of solutions for the Navier-Stokes equations in a three-dimensional, bounded area with periodic boundary conditions. We demonstrate that the solution's maximum derivative norm, when bounded by time and space, remains tied to the initial conditions' derivative norm. This result, combined with the presence of small noise, allows us to prove the solution's distinctiveness regardless of time and space. This research is a continuation of our prior work (Munch and Pausader [2018], Munch and Pausader [2020]]) that addressed the well-posedness of similar systems, and we now address the well-posedness of periodic Navier-Stokes equations in three dimensions.

This paper introduces a new verification protocol for visualizing information, specifically CVQC, which is an efficient and non-interactive verification method for distant settings. CVQC protocol provides a more rapid verification speed in comparison to existing protocols, requiring less computation and interacting solely at the verifier's end. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our protocol through comparative analysis of the CVQC, the original RSMQV, and MQV protocols in terms of transmission distance, hardware, and processing speed. Our results indicate that CVQC surpasses RSMQV and MQV in overall efficiency, particularly by enhancing transmission distance, verifier speed, and chip capacity, and matching or matching or matching the other metrics.

Integrating IoT and blockchain technologies is crucial for creating trustworthy and decentralized systems in various application domains, such as supply chain management and financial transactions. However, traditional blockchain architectures have significant drawbacks when applied to IoT networks, especially in terms of performance. To address this issue, we focus on developing a blockchain architecture tailored for IoT networks and present LC4IoT, a consensus method designed to enhance the scalability and efficiency of blockchain applications on IoT devices. LC4IoT is designed for energy-constrained, resource-limited settings and employs a lightweight consensus protocol to improve performance. Our results demonstrate that LC4IoT is capable of achieving a consensus in less than 1 second on 256 IoT devices while consuming approximately 90 kilobytes of memory. Moreover, LC4IoT's energy efficiency is optimized, allowing it to operate at under 10 kilowatts per consensus. Our research is accompanied by a case study showcasing LC4IoT's adaptability in real-world applications.

For the analysis of cells in images, accurate synthesis of cell shapes is vital.
A novel method is proposed to utilize deep generative models for cell shape
synthesis, which can, in turn, enhance the efficiency of image analysis tasks such
as cell tracking and segmentation by providing reference points for the reconstruction
of missing parts in partial data. To test the method, a diverse dataset of 1.7
million cells from 36 different cell types was used, applying different latent
variables to produce cell shapes according to specific types and cell lineages.
Furthermore, the method demonstrated successful promotion of learned cells by
utilizing prior knowledge from expert cell lines, thereby overcoming issues with
out-of-distribution data. Additionally, the method demonstrated its potential in
recreating cell shapes based on given features, which can be useful in the
reorganization of cell shapes based on parameters such as cell type or lineage.
Lastly, the method successfully incorporated newly acquired images of human red
blood cells that were previously unseen during training, demonstrating its
potential for real-world applications in the advancement of image analysis tasks in
the field of biomedical engineering.

This research paper focuses on developing vision-based techniques to assist internal navigation within visual documents, including haptic documents and visual documents with defective vision. To aid users who cannot access these documents due to vision impairments or limited connectivity, we are working on a cross-platform browser extension to enable smooth reading experiences. Through our initial investigation, we evaluated the current internal navigation methods in scientific and haptic documents but found them inadequate. As a result, we are exploring new techniques combining eye movement detection and deep learning-based methods to create an innovative reference management system. To effectively design this system, we are conducting empirical studies to gather data on users' behaviors and gather opinions from experts. This paper outlines our initial findings, setting the stage for our research approach.

This study serves as a basis for future research on pre-trained language models in the Spanish language, grounded in concerns about bias and variability in model outputs, which can have serious consequences in applications like sentiment analysis. We demonstrate the effectiveness of transferring knowledge from pre-trained English models like BERT and XLNet to the Spanish language, while also highlighting the importance of developing and using pre-trained Spanish models like SPXLNet to achieve better performance in tasks such as sentiment and machine translation analysis.

The discovery of exoplanets around stars other than the Sun, known as Tidal Disruption Stars (TDS), poses challenges in identifying actual planetary effects versus stellar impacts. To overcome these difficulties, we obtained high-resolution spectroscopic data from various sources combining the principles of spectroastrolabex and TDS analyses. By employing the Rossiter-McLaughlin effect and tidal Fourier features, we conducted a four-step analysis. Initially, we identified and quantify the spectral lines of the star and its companion, utilizing synthetic spectra and radial velocity curves. Subsequently, we evaluated the spectral characteristics of the companion star, while simultaneously calculating the radial velocity curves. Notably, the radial velocity curves of the companion stars in TW Hya and LkCa 15 demonstrate distinct differences, allowing us to infer that their orbits can be characterized as Type I and random, respectively. Furthermore, the calculations indicate that the companion star in TW Hya has a mass of 0.504-0.605 MJup, orbiting at a distance of 0.026-0.031 AU, while the companion star in LkCa 15 has a mass of 0.55-0.69 MJup and a highly eccentric orbit with an semi-major axis of 0.14-0.17 AU. These findings indicate that planetary presence is confirmed in TW Hya and LkCa 15, while in LkCa 15, the detected effect is consistent with a planetary solution.
We classify topologically trivial complete metrics with constant curvature on the d-sphere that have conical singularities at a specified set of points.

To understand the hydrodynamics of swimming, we used two advanced computer modeling approaches for a virtual Centipede swimming through a fluid. Our simulations, which combined different fluid models, revealed that wave resistance played a more significant role than inertia in Centipede locomotion, which has significant implications for its actual swimming performance. Our investigation also uncovered distinct, non-Newtonian characteristics of fluid dynamics influencing its movement. Our research demonstrates that wave resistance dominates the Centipede's locomotion, which has important implications for estimating its actual performance. Our study highlights the importance of considering non-Newtonian characteristics to gain a more accurate comprehension of the Centipede's swimming mechanism.

In recent years, tsunami modeling has undergone a significant transformation, shifting its focus from complex mathematical formulations to data-driven approaches that leverage empirical and statistical methods. Yet, despite its adaptability and relatively recent development (the first versions appeared around the year 2000), the adaptive simulation component of these modeling systems remains an underexplored topic. This study aims to fill this knowledge gap by highlighting the key principles of adaptive simulation within the context of tsunami modeling. To illustrate the concept, the research applies the adaptive simulation method to a comprehensive modeling system that integrates various scales, from the depths of the ocean to areas that may be inundated. The modeling system in question utilizes two core components: the non-hydrostatic version of the Navier-Stokes equations, also known as NHHS-Es, and a depth-based approach to model tsunami waves. The research demonstrates the application of the adaptive simulation method by integrating it with both multi-physics multi-domain techniques and multi-scale multi-domain approaches that span from the ocean depths to areas that may be inundated. The study tests the performance of the adaptive simulation method with a real-world tsunami event involving the tsunami that struck Japan on March 11, 2011, caused by the Great East Japan Earthquake. The research setting involves several domains that are each based on a different geographical scale: the ocean domain uses Cartesian coordinates, the near-shore domain uses Triangular Irregular Galerkin (TIGRAS) coordinates, and the area that may be inund

Detecting highly massive galaxies at z>3 is crucial for completing a cosmic census during the reionization epoch. We employed integral field spectroscopy with MUSE on the VLT to identify and study two extremely massive galaxies at z=4.5. These galaxies, which have estimated stellar masses of 1.3x10^11 solar masses, are among the largest objects visible in the optical spectrum that have been identified based on their spectroscopic signatures. Their properties are characterized by starburst activity, significant star formation rates, and a range of measured (Halpha) and predicted (Hbeta+Halpha) star formation efficiencies. Although we cannot determine their exact sizes, their projected angular diameters suggest a rough relationship between mass and physical size. We use our findings to explore the limitations of identifying massive galaxies through spectroscopy, and as part of a larger campaign to investigate how galaxies grow and change in density from redshift 6 to 3.

We have developed a novel framework for seven-dimensional gravity. A
generalized version of the Weyl space theory, this framework incorporates
generalized non-metricity. A specific type of solution within this
framework can replicate the seven-dimensional gyroscope equation when a
specific condition is applied. This equation was initially proposed by Avelino
and Oliveira. A particular rotationally symmetric setup within this
framework corresponds to a 1/2 twisted Sp(8) bosonic string theory background
at the quantum level, analogous to a warped Sp(8) times Sp(1) geometry with
a twisted background. This framework also allows for the creation of killifying
spheres and infinite imbedding Sp(8) bosonic string theory backgrounds at the
quantum level, where the latter replicates a Sp(8) times Sp(1) AdS3, D3
branes scenario with a twisted Sp(8) bosonic string theory background at the
quantum level.

In a study on jamming dynamics in a confined two-dimensional area, 1900 polydisperse disks with diameters from 0.1 to 0.9 and weights from 0.01 to 9, were randomly arranged within a 1.5 by 0.5 meter box. Utilizing a novel method, the disks' positions were inverted to compare jammed configurations. It was observed that using lighter disks in conjunction with larger weights for the thicker disks enhances the disks' mobility in a given configuration, thereby lowering the jamming density. Conversely, employing heavier disks for the thinner ones raises the jamming density. This disk weighting strategy is envisioned to have practical applications in the customization of packing systems.

Research suggests that various types of El Ni\~no (EN) may occur, characterized by distinct precipitation regimes.  La Ni\~na (LN) also exhibits precipitation variations.  Three types of EN and two types of LN have been identified through statistical analysis of atmospheric data, revealing three EN and one hybrid state in the eastern Pacific.  However, our research focuses on hybrid states in the eastern Pacific rather than in prior studies.  Our findings also indicate that two types of LN, denoted as Type I and Type II, have distinct precipitation trends.  The Type I La Ni\~na shows signs of combining with the Warm Line Configuation in the central Pacific, whereas the Type II La Ni\~na appears to be linked with the Cold Slow Convection type.  Our research aims to explore the physical relationships between EN and LN hybrid states and their impacts on Asian precipitation.  Our results indicate that both Type I and Type II La Ni\~na can lead to heavy precipitation in India and may even worsen monsoon failures.  Our study implies that both hybrid states associated with EN may exacerbate precipitation shortages in India.  Our research identifies complex spatial correlations in precipitation patterns linked with EN and LN hybrid states and suggests that investigating hybrid states may offer alternative perspectives on understanding Indian monsoon variability.

Nonaffine models of flexible polymers and random elastic materials have gained acceptance, but their practical application is limited by the unverifiable assumption that nonaffinity persists even in the elastic range. We provide a conditional certification for when this assumption is valid, forming the basis of a relevant question that can be empirically verified through direct observation. We present numerical evidence supporting the existence of nonaffine regions within the elastic range and demonstrate that these areas can become active under specific loads. As a result, we can expect clustering at finite extension lengths. We propose a new decoupling approach that can be used to test the applicability of affine models, even in cases where the materials' microscopic architecture is unknown. This involves comparing the material's actual behavior with that of a simple Gaussian model. By examining both synthetic and real polymer systems, our results indicate the presence of nonaffine regions within the elastic range and suggest that experimentally verifying the conditional certification would readily confirm the occurrence of nonaffinity.

This paper explores two population models, incorporating stochastic elements in a novel framework. The models in question are modified versions of the Basal Skill Model, accounting for training and experience effects as seen in the work of Darroch and others, including work found in the paper's references. The primary connection between these models lies in their shared stochastic structure, despite their differing probability distributions and boundary conditions. The existence of solutions to these probabilistic models is established using semigroups and stochastic processes, providing an understanding of the stochastic basin size. To validate the usefulness of this framework, numerical simulations are performed on a specific model, yielding insights into the influence of training and experience effects on stochastic model behavior, as well as their implications for statistical physics and machine learning research.

This study at present investigates the computational difficulty of fuzzy logic models. Specifically, we concentrate on the issue of whether these models in a specific context called 'fuzzy logic many-valued logic with hedged distributions' are solvable in reasonable time or if solving them necessarily takes a long time. The work builds upon a previous outcome by Bredin, M\'elim\'ee, M\"uller and Schach-Devaat that showed the issue of determining if a fuzzy logic model satisfies certain constraints is complicated. In this work, under a particular assumption about how the model's rules are formulated, we prove that satisfying these constraints is also complicated. In doing so, we gain insight into what makes certain fuzzy logic models computationally feasible and what makes them non-feasible. The work lays out future research directions with a focus on applying these findings to related areas of study.

Taxonomy expansion is a process of automatically adding child concepts to a search query's parent concepts based on their text descriptions. However, existing techniques often suffer from two major drawbacks: they fail to effectively identify relevant child concepts and efficiently expand taxonomies. To address these limitations, we introduce the HyperExpan algorithm, which combines the strengths of two contrasting search methods - ranking and generation - to effectively enlarge taxonomies. The algorithm generates a large pool of potential child concepts using a ranking approach and then leverages a novel generation method to selectively remove less relevant concepts. Our comprehensive evaluation of HyperExpan on five benchmark datasets and taxonomies shows significant improvements over existing techniques in terms of both accuracy and efficiency. Notably, HyperExpan outperforms the best previous technique by a substantial margin, achieving improvements of over 40% in expected search coverage and purity.

A thorough evaluation has been conducted on the performance of various density functional approximations in predicting the electric dipole moment and electric properties of molecular dimers. Research findings indicate that certain DFT-based methods are relatively accurate but show substantial variation among themselves and in comparison to high-level post-Hartree-Fock calculations. A comprehensive analysis of the results reveals that certain parameters significantly influence the accuracy of the predictions, including the choice of density functional, basis set, and bond length. A detailed examination of the effect of the density functional on the results is provided, highlighting potential improvements for future work.

Real-world applications involving uncertainty quantification benefit from addressing both certain and uncertain factors. A typical approach made popular by the coalescing of Bayesian and anti-Bayesian perspectives has gained traction. Nonetheless, in industrial contexts characterized by non-deterministic uncertainties based on component properties, the lack of systematic modeling, the need for manual data analysis, and the insufficiency of modeling for complex system dynamics, necessitate novel methodologies. In an effort to bridge this gap, a novel probabilistic uncertainty modeling approach is introduced, which integrates the method for handling non-deterministic uncertainties based on component properties and is applied to two industrial cases, including a gas turbine system and an aircraft wing. By treating uncertainties arising from component properties as random variables, the proposed approach offers a comprehensive solution, effectively managing complex system dynamics and providing a systematic approach. Moreover, numerical results demonstrate the efficacy of this approach for computing probabilistic outputs such as probability density functions, expected values, and coefficient of variation.

Quantitative analysis of critical systems, particularly in temporal logic, has long been a focus of specification and analysis techniques. However, system specifications regarding resilience, which involves how a system functions in the presence of faults, has been relatively unexplored. There's a lack of clear understanding of how to formally write resilience aspects and translate them into quantitative models for analysis. This paper presents a new methodology for specifying and analyzing system resilience using probabilistic temporal logic, which enables the calculation of a resilience satisfaction value based on performance and recovery times. This value provides an overall measure of a system's ability to recover and operate efficiently, which can facilitate comparative analysis and identification of optimal system configurations.

Despite the substantial evidence for dark matter's presence, its characteristics remain largely unknown. Researchers are exploring novel approaches to detect dark matter due to its elusive nature. Traditional science fiction concepts, like gravitational wave detectors, are being reevaluated for potential applications in space. Our research proposes the use of accelerometers as an early warning system for dark matter-generated gravitational waves in the 10^-7 to 10^-2 Hz frequency range. Our network of accelerometers can simultaneously monitor multiple satellites in different orbits, enhancing our ability to detect dark matter. With several satellites in various orbits, we can cover the 10^-7 to 10^-2 Hz frequency range, offering an effective resolution of a few meters. Our analysis indicates that, with a proper satellite configuration, we can identify dark matter-generated signals from various sources such as galactic halos, globular clusters, and galactic spheroids. Furthermore, we can distinguish between different types of dark matter with varying masses and spatial distributions by measuring the amplitude of the induced signals. Our proposed accelerometer network can offer competitive options for dark matter research, particularly in comparison to established methods like direct detection and indirect detection experiments.

The study offers a quantitative measure of the decay of solutions to the equation $u_t=\Delta^2 u+|x|^2f(u,\Delta u)$ in the exterior of a bounded domain, where $f$ is a given function and $\Delta$ denotes the Laplace operator.

The distribution of polarized radio sources shows a correlation with Faraday rotation measures (RM) in areas with significant magnetic field curvature. This connection is critical in understanding the relationship between magnetic field properties and polarized emission from radio sources. By analyzing the curvature of the low-frequency radio spectrum, we can infer the median polarization of radio sources and derive constraints on the magnetic field properties. This study only considers narrow-line RM data, excluding broad-line sources and those with unstable RM values. After applying a correction for curved magnetic field models, we recalculated the polarization slope for 173 high-polarization radio sources. Compared to a flat model, the curved model shows preferential agreement with the data at a confidence level of 90%, resulting in a specific value of $\beta_{100\rm{mG}}=-(2.1\pm0.3)\sigma^{-4.4}$.

The updated three-dimensional RM equation includes terms representing the curvature of the magnetic field, with $\alpha$ indicating the curvature's degree and $\beta$ relating curvature to polarization. By applying a curved model, we can derive $\beta$ as $\beta_{100\rm{mG}}=-(2.1\pm0.3)\sigma^{-4.4}$. After adjusting for cosmological effects, the 3D RM volume is calculated as $V_{\rm{RM,3D}}=(4.0\pm0.6)\pm(1.2\pm0.

To quantify the uncertainty in a probabilistic event, several entropy metrics can be utilized. Nevertheless, selecting the right entropy metric is crucial because different metrics can lead to contradictory conclusions when assessing the same system's uncertainty. Research has previously suggested employing maximal entropy metrics. In this study, the use of minimal entropy metrics is explored as an alternative approach to measure uncertainty. Specifically, a method based on interpolation is proposed to compare the minimal entropy metric with other entropy metrics. By numerically solving the interpolation equation, the relationship between minimal and maximal entropy metrics can be determined, potentially providing insights to aid in the selection of an appropriate entropy metric. Furthermore, this study demonstrates how the interpolation method can be applied to quantify the uncertainty in a specific physical system, namely, the Majumdar-Shastry spin chain, which has an exact solution, thus allowing for a precise verification of its convergence.

The subscale energy cascade in turbulent flows within the hyperdiffusive framework is re-examined. It is argued that the associated transport operator can be expressed as the product of subscale periodic structures and related subscale velocity auto-correlation. This concept is further applied to develop subgrid-scale energy closure based on periodic subscales, with closure terms accounting for subscale periodic structure modulation. This approach aligns with high-order hyperdiffusive models, also known as Smagorinskii model extensions, and has the additional benefit of incorporating extra unknowns into the SGS closure, similar to the original Smagorinskii model, which includes the turbulent Prandtl number and a length scale. Specifically, the subgrid-scale energy closure extends the Smagorinskii closure as it now includes three new unknowns: the turbulent Prandtl number, a length scale, and the fraction of total energy addressed by the model. This approach also allows for the determination of subscale structures or 'periodic patterns' within turbulent flows. Computational simulations using LES show the proposed closure achieves good results for homogeneous, isotropic, and high-speed flows.

Conventional approaches to analyzing elastic scattering data have significant limitations due to the numerous complex potentials involved in phase-shift analysis and the uncertainty in phase shift energy dependencies during resonant SPI. This paper introduces a novel technique to fit consistently consistent experimental data and naturally incorporate multiple complex potentials, featuring consistent SPI and the Drury model's diffractive oxidation reduction, with parameters such as optical potential surfaces, diffractive parameters, and spin-orbit terms able to be derived through the analysis of observed observables including multipole polarization and parity non-conservation. This method was applied to the elastic scattering of 7Li on 208Pb in an investigation that included new experimental data collected over several years, resulting in consistent analysis of the observables and systematics, and the emergence of a new method to determine the optical model parameters.

In boundary field theory, the concepts of thermodynamics are often utilized, yet certain boundary effects are rarely considered when modeling blackbody thermodynamics. We've investigated two topics where boundary influences are crucial: the geometric variation of temperature, which doesn't rely on the frequency of a given scenario, and the frequency-dependent thermal conductivity of an electromagnetic blackbody cavity.

The former involves demonstrating that commonly employed techniques for frequency-dependent calculations, such as the dispersion relation method, introduce artificial frequency-dependent elements that aren't present in the genuine frequency-independent geometric variation. Additionally, we found that the standard formulas used to calculate spatially varying temperatures contain discrepancies.

The latter explores electromagnetic cavity thermodynamics, which serves as an extension to a previously examined topic. We've investigated two configurations - a rectangular cavity with a small removal and a slab conductor - emphasizing the importance of boundary conditions on thermodynamic quantity definitions. Notably, the presence of boundary conditions necessitates the introduction of additional dynamical elements, which in turn complicates the frequency-dependent thermal conductivity of the slab conductor.

We've established a set of non-trivial, frequency-dependent boundary conditions for both magnetic dipole and electric dipole modes within the slab conductor, which allows for accurate frequency-dependent conductivity even in the absence of a complete dynamical model. This understanding can potentially enable the development of a dynamical model, which is a crucial step in further research.

The proliferation of intelligent devices has led to abundant data, including sensitive information, prompting a need for proactive measures to safeguard privacy. Location-based services, in particular, pose significant privacy risks due to the high-resolution data, extensive coverage, and diverse datasets, yielding substantial privacy losses. The challenges of depersonalizing data while maintaining user anonymity in order to safeguard individual privacy are key difficulties in accomplishing this goal. Assuming knowledge of private objects in a location-based setting doesn't affect, doesn't affect knows privacy loss when dealing with dependent data, whereas other approaches do. To address this issue, a location-based system incorporating a Bayesian hierarchical model and a deep neural network representation is proposed. The approach depersonalizes data based on its anonomyzation level and replaces it with fake data at various levels, while preserving depersonalized data with high anonomyzation levels. This paper introduces a novel method for generating a geometrically informed 3D point cloud representation that facilitates place recognition and 3D localization. The new representation, called a 3D neural density field (3DNDF), employs a neural network to map point clouds into a compact, 3D occupancy field with 8 voxels. This transformation simplifies point cloud analysis by converting an unordered set of 3D points into a structured, volumetric occupancy structure. Adapting the voxelization process from 2D to 3D improves geometric robustness in point clouds, especially in cases with high depth noise. The 3DNDF representation enhances the efficiency of place recognition using 3D point clouds and supports both localization and recognition tasks through its compact, volumetric structure. Experimental results demonstrate the success of our 3DNDF representation in both top-down view and 3D-based place recognition and localization, outperforming existing point-set registration and learning-based methods.

The precise evaluation (inference) of differences between brain networks in distinct groups relies heavily on the accurate modeling of inter-site variability (influence of each brain site). Inter-site variability plays a significant role in understanding differences between groups, thus raising important questions about the influence of known factors, such as group labels, on inter-site effects. In this study, we investigated the impact of group labels on inter-site effects using a statistical model, referred to as the brain connectivity model (BCM), which incorporates several key concepts. Firstly, we established that the BCM can distinguish between large differences caused by group labels. Secondly, we identified that individual and group differences are reliably identified when inter-site effects are substantial due to group influences. However, when inter-site effects are primarily driven by random factors, differences between groups become less distinguishable. Our research provides critical insights into the significance of inter-site effects in understanding brain connectivity and highlights the limitations of statistical inference at the network level due to substantial variability between random factors.

In the context of the efficient private computation problem on a distributed network with two stations, we examine the naming and counting issues. The goal is to process a binary input held by each station into a binary output using local operations while maintaining communication privacy. Our focus lies on the naming problem, where stations aim to produce the same binary value, and the counting problem, where stations aim to produce a value indicating the number of ones in the combined input. For these challenges, we have developed algorithms with energy complexity polynomial in $n$, the number of stations, using $n^2$-degree randomness. Notably, our algorithms exhibit the same communication complexity and error rate as the current best methods, although our naming algorithm achieves improved interaction at higher levels of error. Additionally, our counting algorithm reduces interaction at lower levels of error compared to the current best methods, although our naming algorithm undergoes an opposite change. The algorithms we have developed are based on a new, relevant application of the Gilbreth random walk concept.

This paper presents a novel encoding approach that integrates the inherent structure of code-mixed languages to enhance the performance of pre-trained and fine-tuned language models. The proposed method starts by defining a graph representation capturing the intrinsic code-mixing pattern. It then develops a novel positional encoding technique that distills the graph into a linear representation and encodes it for cross-lingual neural machine translation tasks. The proposed encoding technique is versatile and can be applied to multiple positional encoding methods. The application of our encoding technique to the handling of positionally-dependent tasks in a multi-task setting yields significant gains of 3.2 and 2.5 BLEU points over state-of-the-art models in English-to-Hindi and Hindi-to-English translation, respectively.

To understand the contribution of isotopes to the disordering of hydrogen in H$_{3}$S at high pressure and low temperature, we utilized density functional theory to calculate the isotope effect coefficient ($\delta$) within the framework of Ehrenfest's second order theory. Our calculations reveal that $\delta$ is composed of two components generated by the vibrational frequency ($\nu$) and Born-Oppenheimer coupling ($\gamma$), each exhibiting distinct behaviors under pressure. While $\delta_{\nu}$ decreases with pressure, $\delta_{\gamma}$ displays the opposite trend, initially rising before eventually decreasing. The variation of $\delta$ generated by Born-Oppenheimer coupling has important implications for its role in the percolation of percolating hydrogen, suggesting that Born-Oppenheimer coupling may play a more significant part in process than previously contemplated. By investigating how the two components evolve with pressure, we are able to identify a critical pressure of 140 GPa at which Born-Oppenheimer coupling takes over as the primary source of isotope effect coefficient, a shift that occurs prior to reaching high-pressure hydrogen dissociation (H$_{3}$S$\rightarrow$HS$^{-}$) pressure of 250 GPa.

This research introduces SpatialGIMP, a modified version of the Growth-Based Motion Planning algorithm that leverages spatial constraints to streamline navigation in crowded environments. SpatialGIMP generates personalized spatial constraints for each agent based on their relative positions, speed, and desired pathways, to prioritize safe proximity and flow. To integrate these constraints into GIMP's motion planning process, the paper revises the algorithm's cost function and collision avoidance mechanism. SpatialGIMP was put through its paces using the SUMO and ApolloS2S simulation platforms, testing against popular trajectory planning methods. Results show that SpatialGIMP successfully maintains safe distances while outperforming other methods in various metrics, including flow, density, and collision-free success rates.

Building on the success of learning-based methods in 3D vision, we introduce a method for learning object descriptors that improves camera pose estimation, particularly in scenarios where object descriptors are affected by changes in lighting, materials, and texture. Traditional descriptors rely on hand-designed patterns but these are vulnerable in certain conditions. In contrast, our descriptors are learned from example images and are optimized for hand-designed templates as well as descriptor metrics like robustness and uniqueness. The learning process is grounded in theory with a bilinear model for shape and pattern optimization. The technique performs well across multiple datasets and conditions, outperforming existing methods.

In a multiuser MIMO communication system with 2 users, where each is equipped with 4 transmit and receive antennas, we apply two variants of group LASSO, using different loss functions, to mitigate co-channel interference and solve a generalized version of the Beamforming Game. This formulation incorporates users with distinct QoS requirements and a network power constraint. By applying the group LASSO to the sum of a beamforming vector and interference management vector, we resolve the game by solving two convex problems. This approach offers improved outcomes in terms of sum-rate and interference management compared to traditional LASSO and Benchmark methods.

Given a finite harmonic map $\pi: \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{B}$ between tropical curves $\mathcal{C}$ and $\mathcal{B}$, we investigate the pull-back of rational functions on $\mathcal{C}$ to rational functions on $\mathcal{B}$, and show that this pull-back fails in general for the semifield of rational functions. However, we introduce a novel extension of rational functions that makes the pull-back work for any pair of tropical curves with finite harmonic maps between them. Additionally, we demonstrate that our new construction aligns with previous extensions of rational functions in certain specific scenarios. Furthermore, we utilize tropical geometry methods to provide an alternative proof of Kapranov's non-degeneracy condition for the Jacobian of tropical curves.

This research ensures the existence and uniqueness of a quasi-stationary distribution for a Markov process when observed over a continuous, bounded, and smooth area in time. Specifically, we consider Bessel processes and prove that a quasi-stationary distribution exists and is unique when considering processes that spend a given amount of time near the boundary of a certain ball for a sufficient period. This is established under a specific condition that involves the'speed of convergence' towards the boundary, which in the case of Bessel processes relies on the specific nature of the Bessel process itself. For processes that spend a similar amount of time near the boundary of a specific 'pocket' area in a generalised Ornstein-Ulenbeck process, we establish the existence and uniqueness of a quasi-stationary distribution under a specific condition that involves the specific nature of this process itself. This research provides insight into the specific nature of the generalised Ornstein-Ulenbeck process when 'weakly interacting' with a specific type of Poisson point process, which describes the behaviour of a generalised Ornstein-Ulenbeck process when there are a small number of 'ultra-weak' interactions.

Building on the findings of Agol and Swenson, we demonstrate that integral knot invariants can be derived by integrating specific cocycles, which generates fresh cocycles of an alternate nature, and we establish the connection to Agol--Swenson and Walker's work on ideal cocycles, focusing particularly on branched hyperbolic knots in three-spheres.

Our research employs elastoresistance measurements to investigate the dynamic
properties of nafeas and LiFeAs near their respective transition temperatures.
Analysis of the NaFeAs elastoresistance shows a substantial enhancement at
(100) symmetry, and this increase drops off as frequency gets lower, indicating
the symmetry has a specific relationship with spin fluctuations. Similarly, our
LiFeAs elastoresistance also displays a significant enhancement at (110) symmetry
but, in contrast, its low-frequency behavior is the opposite; it increases instead
of decreases, which indicates spin fluctuations have a more intricate relationship
with the low-frequency elastoresistance in LiFeAs. Furthermore, the comparison
between nafeas and LiFeAs shows that fluctuations in LiFeAs have a more moderate
response and are generally the lowest they can be. Lastly, our research also
shows that elastoresistance can be controlled by strain allowing it to act as a
strain-sensitive detector which in turn can be used to identify magnetic
phenomena in iron-based materials.

In this study, we have thoroughly examined a broad class of Type-II two Higgs doublet models, considering multiple theoretical restrictions, including mesh regularization of the tree-level Higgs potential power expansion, the vacuum stability condition, the perturbative unity constraint, and the requirement for a longer live of the Higgs boson. Several model parameters were constrained by allowing variations in the other model parameters. The results show that, after imposing all the theoretical restrictions, the allowed parameter space for the Higgs boson's decay into a Z boson and an intermediate boson is severely limited, with the bulk and mirror scales falling within specific range constraints. Our findings also indicate that the Higgs boson's coupling strength remains within a narrow percentage range, %0.22, while its decay rate into a Z boson and an A boson remains within a narrow percentage range, %0.58, of the standard model prediction. These findings are also applicable to the related scenario in which the Higgs boson decays into a Z boson and a lighter, additional Higgs boson.

In the field of architectural academia, a novel learning approach is proposed to derive morphological optimization criteria from disparate static and dynamic states. A neural network, trained on data extracted from COMSOL simulations and animated sequences, learns to distinguish between intentionally and unintentionally derived design specifications. Intentional criteria, based on user-defined objectives, prioritize mechanical characteristics extracted from COMSOL analysis, whereas unintentional criteria, stemming from unsupervised exploration, focus on visual stimuli from animated sequences. A method for automatically assigning weights to specific specificities is presented, allowing for precise prioritization of criteria derived from either source. A case study demonstrates the efficacy of this optimized set of specificities in guiding micro-exploratory design procedures, resulting in innovative composite material configurations.

Flavor-symmetric confining vacua in chiral gauge theories must satisfy the 't Hooft anomaly matching equations, which pose a challenge for the same vacua. We investigate whether these equations allow for consistent quantum mechanics, focusing on a chiral gauge theory with a single fermion delocalized in flavor and space-time. In this context, we derive a necessary condition for the theory to have a consistent quantum mechanics by examining the anomalies related to reductive Lie algebras and demonstrate that no non-trivial flavor-symmetric confining vacua meet this requirement. We further show that even when considering theory-agnostic anomalies, those related to reductive Lie algebras are sufficient to preclude the existence of non-trivial flavor-symmetric confining vacua. The same analysis, applied to theories with additional degrees of freedom, results in a negative conclusion for their existence as well.

We establish the well-posedness of the Navier-Stokes equations in certain homogeneous Triebel-Lizorkin spaces by leveraging the use of the Littlewood-Paley projections and by demonstrating the existence of a bounded $L^p$-$L^q$ maximal regularity for the Stokes equations in these spaces.

A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to study the interaction between thermal magnons and light in the context of antiferromagnetic materials with a specific symmetry. By applying this model to a particular type of antiferromagnet known as strontium iridate, researchers demonstrated that certain modes within the material's magnon spectrum exhibit a relationship with the direction of their electronic spin. Furthermore, temperature-dependent studies of these magnon modes reveal distinct changes in their resonance frequencies and intensities, showcasing the material's capacity to be modulated by heat. Such controllability over the interaction between heat and light in these materials presents promising prospects for the development of photonic systems that can withstand extreme temperatures.

Quantum-based proposals for public-key encryption and decryption have garnered attention due to potential SUPERC encryption advantages. However, the inherent no-cloning theorem complication necessitates a direct measurement of the transmitted quantum state, thus compromising its unknown, random nature. We present a new SUPERC approach that preserves the transmitted quantum state's randomness, achieved through introduction of a carefully controlled, randomized phase shift. By applying a set of specific, randomized rotations to the transmitted qubit, we ensure its randomness remains intact. The proposed modifications require minimal modifications to the SUPERC protocol, yielding benefits including reduced public-key sizes, increased transmission efficiency, and operational stability. Notably, the additional phase shift can be generated using a single qubit, further enhancing SUPERC's practicality.

Language models have reached remarkable precision, yet they continue to struggle understanding the significance of uncommon words in their vocabulary. To enhance their rare word representation, we suggest a method where we guide the models to learn these words by using their definitions rather than relying solely on instances from the training data. The process commences with an analysis of our method to pinpoint suitable language models, then an evaluation follows to assess the effectiveness of our approach using a range of measures. The results demonstrate that our technique results in more precise representations of rare words in line with their definitions. Furthermore, we discovered that incorporating your own dictionary can lead to better understanding of words not present in the model's training data. Additionally, we found that rare word representation improvement can result in an enhancement to their overall understanding.

For a weighted graph with independent edge weights and a specific distribution, we find that the extremal weights of a random Minimum Spanning Acyclic Graph converge in probability for a particular edge weight distribution, demonstrating a type of law of large numbers. By building on this finding, we establish the convergence of extremal weights for a random Minimum Weight Perfect Matching and explore similar results for other types of minimum-weight substructures in bipartite graphs.

This study presents a novel vertical FL protocol called Splitting-Based Vertical Federated Learning (SB-VFL), which addresses privacy concerns by combining differential privacy and privacy attacks removal techniques to protect against sensitive information exposure (SIE) and sensitive data inference (SDI) attacks. A comprehensive evaluation framework incorporating seven data inference attacks into the PLINDO benchmark suite demonstrates that SB-VFL effectively prevents SIE and SDI attacks while maintaining satisfactory model performance for classification tasks. Moreover, the proposed protocol is adaptable to different privacy budgets and achieves significant improvements in privacy without substantial compromises in accuracy.

Utilizing the $B$-quark light-cone sum rules, researchers examined the $B^+ o p \bar{\Psi}$ decay width, where $\Psi$ represents either the $J/P$-wave $\chi_{c1}(1P)$ or $\chi_{c2}(1P)$ charmonium states. In the process, it was discovered that the decay width of $B^+ o p \bar{\Psi}$ significantly depends on the mass and effective coupling of a dark antibaryon resulting from the light-discussed dark matter particle $\chi$ interacting with quarks, which was initially proposed in \cite{Agasiz:2021rzs}. With specific values of $\gamma_q=1.32$ and $M_D=1021$ GeV for the dark antibaryon mass, the calculated decay widths for $B^+ o p \bar{\Psi}$, where $\Psi$ is the $J/P$-wave $\chi_{c1}(1P)$ or $\chi_{c2}(1P)$ charmonium states, were found to be $[7.53^{+1.87}_{-1.63}]$ and $[11.58^{+3.94}_{-3.41}]$ femtometers, respectively. These results were obtained assuming that the charm quark mass is 1.58 GeV and the kinetic energy parameter $\mu_{\chi}^2$

In the event of an unforeseen terrorist attack, the strategic allocation of limited resources such as military units and protective devices, poses significant challenges for government agencies. Our study tackles this complex issue by developing a coordinated resource distribution system that enables various government entities to work synergistically towards common objectives. In this research, we utilize a game-theoretic approach to design resource allocation policies that foster cooperation among government agencies, as well as an adaptive method to address interagency resource allocation. Interestingly, our findings reveal that tailored allocation strategies specifically designed to defend against terrorist threats can be replicated through an autonomous decision-making process that prioritizes agencies' needs in hierarchical order, with agencies responsible for smaller threats prioritizing defense over those responsible for larger threats. Furthermore, our proposed model and analysis highlight key resource allocation patterns. Our data-driven analysis indicates that these proposed resource allocation strategies are applicable not only to the case without prior knowledge but also when agencies have access to uncertain information about potential threats. Our study utilizes the United States as a reference point, with our model and analysis tailored to account for the unique characteristics and interagency relationships of American city governments.

This study explores the thermodynamic properties and phase transition behavior of a spherical cavity comprised of a charged black fluid in the presence of an electric field. The research utilizes the model of the Einstein-Maxwell-Bianchi perfect fluid dynamics interacting with electromagnetic radiation. A model for the cavity's boundary is introduced, and its interior space is defined by a series of modified Bianchi type-I metrics that incorporate electric charge. The momentum currents on the boundary are specified, and the stress tensor's tangential components are determined, revealing that the system exhibits isotropic properties. A matching condition is applied to derive a set of equations that integrate the system's energy and momentum, yielding a complete set of models for the cavity's spacetime. One such model, corresponding to vanishing shear and the perfect fluid assumption, simplifies to the model of Schwarzschild-de Sitter, revealing that the cavity's boundary corresponds to its event horizon. The researchers found that for this model, the cavity's interior space corresponds to the anti-de Sitter model. Another model, corresponding to the assumption of zero electric charge, simplifies to the model of Schwarzschild. The researchers used these spacetime models to calculate various thermodynamic parameters for the cavity, including black holes, and examined their phase transition behavior. The results indicate that the phase transition behavior of the cavity's interior space is significantly influenced by the electric potential.

This research introduces a new sampling approach called bag sampling, designed to enhance the scalability of bag bag bag models in ranking tasks. By employing a novel estimator, the method reduces memory consumption and increases the model's parallelization capabilities, enabling it to rank longer documents more efficiently. Building on this foundation, the study achieves state-of-the-art results in ranking longer documents by developing the ROUGE-inspired bag sampling (RIBS) model, which improves over previous state-of-the-art models on the Google WMT data set. Furthermore, the work investigates the effectiveness of bag models in ranking shorter documents and proposes the lightweight bag model, lightweight bag with ranking (LWR), demonstrating that bag models can be optimized for shorter documents as well, yielding superior performance on the Wikipedia data set compared to the state-of-the-art models.

Graph Neural Networks have achieved significant success in semi-supervised node classification tasks. A key benefit of GNNs is their ability to capitalize on unlabeled data through a graph construction process. Nevertheless, when this unlabeled data is labeled via machine learning, errors are inevitably introduced, which can substantially undermine the semi-supervised node classification process. Building upon the observation that traditional pseudo-labeling methods utilize probability-based thresholds to label unlabeled data, which often leads to considerable label noise, we propose the Graph Pseudo-Labeling method, which seeks to optimize the threshold by considering both neighborhood expansion and labeling costs. Experimental results show that our method outperforms other pseudo-labeling methods, which were modified to incorporate the neighborhood expansion technique, in multiple scenarios on established datasets. Moreover, the efficacy of our method is further substantiated through experiments on real-world datasets, which also reveal that it offers improved scalability compared to other approaches.

The plasma wakefield acceleration technique utilizing betatron radiation, independent of particle energy, has the potential to be an uncorrelated source of intense gamma rays.
